findings.issue: withdraw() gates its side effects on withdrawal.withdrawn (the scopes this call newly flipped) instead of on the resulting consent state. withdraw_consent() has already COMMITTED the consent row (consent_store.py:137) before disable_auto_apply (line 41) and execute_deletion (line 45) run, and those two calls are outside that transaction. If either raises - tenant connection error, validate_schema_name ValueError on a malformed schema_name, a commit failure inside _soft_delete - the consent row is durably persisted but the side effect never happens and the caller gets a 500. A retry is then permanently a no-op: consent_store.withdraw_consent computes newly = scopes still True, finds none, returns Withdrawal(withdrawn=()), so the router answers 200 with {"withdrawn": [], "account_deletion": null} while auto_apply_enabled is still True and the account was never deactivated or scheduled for deletion (AC8/AC10 silently unsatisfied, with a success response). There is no other code path that re-drives these effects. The area is flagged high-risk by specs/brownfield/risk-map.md R11 (legally load-bearing consent machinery), and tests/unit/test_consent_service.py:98 (test_a_repeated_withdrawal_triggers_nothing_again) pins the broken behaviour, so no existing test would fail if the defect were present.
findings.fix: Drive the side effects from the post-withdrawal record rather than from the delta: replace `if "auto_apply" in withdrawal.withdrawn` with `if not withdrawal.record.consented_to_auto_apply` and `if "data_processing" in withdrawal.withdrawn` with `if not withdrawal.record.consented_to_data_processing`. Both helpers are already idempotent (disable_auto_apply no-ops when the pref is already False; _soft_delete just re-sets is_active/audits), so a retry completes the withdrawal. Update test_a_repeated_withdrawal_triggers_nothing_again to assert the side effects DO re-run on retry while no new consent row or audit event is written.

findings.issue: GET /api/consent derives `current` as `history[-1]` (last element of the consent_history ASC list) rather than calling consent_store.current_consent. The codebase now has two independent definitions of "the latest consent": ORDER BY consented_at ASC then take the last, versus ORDER BY consented_at DESC LIMIT 1. With duplicate consented_at values (or after the ordering issue in CRA-003) the two can disagree, so the user could be shown flags that differ from the ones apply_matched_jobs actually enforces. It is also duplicated logic the diff could have reused.
findings.fix: Call `await consent_store.current_consent(user.id, db)` for the `current` field and keep consent_history only for the `history` list, so display and enforcement read the record through the same query.

findings.issue: Which record is 'current' is decided entirely by consented_at, and consented_at is generated in Python by whichever process writes the row (_withdrawal_row passes datetime.now(timezone.utc); record_consent relies on the model's Python-side default). docker-compose runs app, worker and beat as separate containers, so a withdrawal written by a host whose clock trails the one that wrote the grant sorts BEFORE the grant; current_consent then returns the stale grant and apply_matched_jobs keeps processing after a valid withdrawal. Nothing in the diff guards against a non-monotonic consented_at, and the ORDER BY has no tie-breaker.
findings.fix: Let the database clock order the rows: pass `consented_at=sa.func.now()` in _withdrawal_row (and/or give ConsentRecord.consented_at a `server_default=func.now()`), so all rows are stamped by the single Postgres clock. Cheapest alternative: add a monotonic sequence column and order by it.

findings.issue: Consent is read once at the top of _inner and never re-read. The per-job loop (lines 166-281) then runs up to apply_cap_daily iterations, each doing parse_master_resume + generate_tailored_resume + generate_cover_letter (LLM provider calls with the user's resume) and a live portal submission - minutes of work. A withdrawal of llm_processing or auto_apply that lands mid-run is not honoured for the remainder of the batch, so the user's data continues to reach the LLM provider after they exercised DPDP s.6(4). No test covers a withdrawal arriving mid-run.
findings.fix: Re-read consent inside the loop before the tailoring block: `consent = await consent_store.current_consent(user_id, shared_db)` then `if _consent_refused(user_id, consent, "llm_processing"): break` immediately before the parse_master_resume call (and the same for "auto_apply" before apply_to_job).

findings.issue: AC5's core claim - that SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serialises concurrent withdrawals so neither copies a stale flag back to True - is never executed. The unit test (tests/unit/test_consent_withdrawal.py:157) only asserts that the compiled SQL string ends with 'FOR UPDATE'; it does not prove the lock is held across the read and the insert, and the FakeDB has no transaction at all. The only real-PostgreSQL test is skipped unless RUN_DB_TESTS=1 (and the context pack confirms it was not run), and even that test issues the two withdrawals sequentially via separate sessions - never concurrently - despite its docstring claiming 'the user row lock is taken'.
findings.fix: Add one concurrency case to test_consent_withdrawal_db.py: open two sessions, run withdraw_consent(['auto_apply']) and withdraw_consent(['llm_processing']) with asyncio.gather, and assert the final current_consent has BOTH flags False and exactly two new rows exist. Also drop or substantiate the 'user row lock is taken' claim in the module docstring.

findings.issue: `account_deletion: dict[str, Any] | None` puts an untyped Any-valued dict in a public API response model. CLAUDE.md mandates 'Static typing everywhere (zero any)', and the response contract for the deletion summary is left unspecified for clients and unverifiable by mypy. The rest of the module is precisely typed, so this is local drift.
findings.fix: Add `class DeletionSummary(BaseModel): mode: str; message: str; hard_delete_after: str` and type the field `DeletionSummary | None`; the router can construct it from the execute_deletion dict. app/compliance/deletion.py itself stays unchanged.

findings.issue: On the idempotent no-op path withdraw_consent returns after taking the FOR UPDATE lock on the users row without committing or rolling back, so the row lock is held until the caller's session is closed (get_db's finally). Harmless in the current short request, but it silently blocks a concurrent withdrawal for the rest of the request lifetime.
findings.fix: `await db.commit()` before the `return Withdrawal(record=latest, withdrawn=())` to release the lock. Do not use rollback - it would expire the User instance loaded by get_current_user and turn the later `user.schema_name` read into a lazy refresh on an async session.

findings.issue: The set of valid scopes is declared twice: CONSENT_SCOPES here and the ConsentScope Literal in app/schemas/consent.py:7. _checked_scopes raises a bare ValueError that the router does not catch (it would surface as a 500); it is unreachable today only because the Literal happens to match. Drift is caught by test_consent.py:66, which keeps this at INFO.
findings.fix: Derive the Literal from the mapping, e.g. `ConsentScope = Literal[tuple(CONSENT_SCOPES)]` via typing, or catch ValueError in the router and return 422.

findings.issue: Beyond the one line CHG-007 needs (`app.include_router(consent.router)` plus the `consent` import), the whole import block is re-sorted and `import sys`/`import asyncio` are swapped - drive-by reformatting unrelated to the story. tests/unit/test_consent_store.py's import was likewise reflowed with no behavioural change. This inflates the diff a reviewer must read against the surgical-change principle.
findings.fix: No action required if the repo-wide ruff isort pass is an accepted separate commit (4a522c4); keep such reformatting out of feature commits in future.

findings.issue: _consent_refused reads as a pure predicate but emits a structlog line and an audit event as a side effect of being asked a question. The docstring says so, but a caller adding a second check would silently double-audit. Also note apply_matched_jobs still gets dispatched by auto_apply_for_all_users for every active user who has withdrawn, so each beat tick writes another consent.enforced row - that is what AC8 asks for, but the audit volume grows with the beat schedule, not with user action.
findings.fix: Optional: rename to refuse_and_audit(), or split the audit call out of the predicate. If audit volume matters, filter withdrawn users in auto_apply_for_all_users before dispatch.
